overview: The atlas calls this layer “English territory” from 1279 to 1492. Its polygon combines much of England, sampled Welsh areas, almost all Ireland, and Gascony around Bordeaux and Bayonne. The shape repeats in 1279, 1300, and 1400. It is a modern editorial layer, not a contemporary country name or surveyed border. It excludes Tintagel, Conwy, and Calais while including Dublin, Cork, Bordeaux, and Bayonne. The Irish component especially needs caution: late-medieval English authority was concentrated in particular lordships, towns, and the Pale rather than evenly covering the island. The 1492 map removes this exact id. Its sampled English and Welsh locations plus Dublin and Cork become “england-1492,” while Bordeaux and Bayonne become France; the assignments persist in 1500. The boundary therefore changes both label and territorial story at a software seam. This card treats the shape as a navigation aid, then localizes evidence to named places, institutions, and communities. Its chapters follow political change, families, childhood, work, trade, medicine, sanitation, writing, faith, craft, and continuity without pretending that one color created one shared daily life.

periods.title: 1279 to 1290: conquest and expulsion
periods.summary: Edward I’s forces conquered Gwynedd in 1282 and 1283, then castle building helped enforce a new political order in north Wales. In England, Jewish families faced escalating discrimination before the crown expelled the entire Jewish community in 1290 and seized property.

periods.title: 1290 to 1307: castles, taxes, and Parliament
periods.summary: The crown needed money for war, so assemblies became important places to seek consent for taxation. The 1295 Parliament included knights and burgesses. At Beaumaris, meanwhile, castle construction began after Llanfaes residents were forced to move, making monumental architecture somebody else’s eviction notice.

periods.title: 1307 to 1327: years of hunger
periods.summary: Repeated harvest failure from 1315 brought the Great Famine, followed by cattle plague and severe mortality through 1322. Hunger was not one bad dinner: it meant years of shrinking reserves, dear food, disease, and loss. The crisis crossed reigns, households, manors, and towns unevenly.

periods.title: 1327 to 1348: wool, ports, and war with France
periods.summary: Edward III’s government drew customs revenue from trade, especially wool, while merchants moved cloth, wine, and other goods through ports. The Hundred Years War began in 1337. A kingdom financing war through commerce tied distant sheep pastures, warehouses, ships, taxpayers, and battlefields together.

periods.title: 1348 to 1360: plague and a contested labor market
periods.summary: The Black Death reached England in 1348 and killed an enormous share of the population. With workers scarce, survivors could seek better terms. Parliament’s 1351 Statute of Labourers tried to restrain wages and movement, showing rulers attempting to push society back toward pre-plague expectations.

periods.title: 1360 to 1381: taxes, labor rules, and revolt
periods.summary: Plague recurred, war costs continued, and authorities kept trying to regulate labor. A poll tax charged most people over fifteen in 1381. Its collection helped ignite a broad revolt whose participants attacked records and officials, demanded change, and forced royal government into a frightening confrontation.

periods.title: 1381 to 1399: negotiation, rebellion, and deposition
periods.summary: Richard II’s rule survived the revolt but ended in deposition. In Ireland during 1394 and 1395, the king negotiated submissions from many Gaelic lords through interpreters and formal oaths. The quick unraveling of that settlement exposes how little the atlas’s solid Irish color explains.

periods.title: 1399 to 1422: Lancastrians, worship, art, and war
periods.summary: Henry IV began a Lancastrian dynasty, while Henry V’s campaigns culminated at Agincourt in 1415. At York, John Thornton’s team made the vast Great East Window after a 1405 commission. War, parish worship, pilgrimage, skilled craft, and royal politics shared the same generation.

periods.title: 1422 to 1453: minority rule and the loss of Gascony
periods.summary: Henry VI became king as a baby. Political competition grew while English positions in France contracted. Bordeaux fell in 1453, ending effective English rule in Gascony, although the atlas keeps its southwest-France polygon colored “English territory” until 1492 and thereby stretches one possession thirty-nine years too long.

periods.title: 1453 to 1492: dynastic war, print, and Tudor rule
periods.summary: The Wars of the Roses repeatedly displaced kings and harmed communities without turning every year into nonstop battle. William Caxton established a press at Westminster in 1476. Henry VII won at Bosworth in 1485, and the atlas changes ids in 1492 during his continuing reign.

sections.title: Read this atlas shape before trusting its color

items.text: The exact index supplies one generated id, “english-territory,” with the display name “English territory” and approximate dates 1279 to 1492. It is absent in 1200 and has no imported summary, accepted override, or indexed card. Those are software facts, not proof that medieval people used this phrase as a country name.

The 1279 feature is a MultiPolygon with three components: much of England and sampled Welsh areas, almost all Ireland, and southwest France around Bordeaux and Bayonne. London, York, Cardiff, Dublin, Cork, Bordeaux, and Bayonne fall inside; sampled Tintagel, Conwy, Edinburgh, Calais, Jersey, and the Isle of Man do not.

The decoded 1279 and 1300 geometries are exactly identical. The 1400 file keeps the same 235 positions and sampled membership, but small coordinate-conversion drift changes its hash. That is technical encoding noise, not evidence that the coastlines and frontiers historically moved together.

The Irish polygon is especially misleading. Richard II had to negotiate submissions from many Gaelic lords through interpreters in 1394 and 1395, and the settlement soon unraveled. A solid color covering nearly all Ireland therefore cannot mean one uniform law, tax system, language, or everyday allegiance.

At the 1492 seam, sampled English and Welsh points plus the atlas’s Irish probes switch to “england-1492,” while Bordeaux and Bayonne switch to France. The kingdom did not reboot when a JSON file changed ids. Henry VII had already ruled since 1485, so this is a labeling seam under the same king.

sections.title: See how power worked through kings, assemblies, courts, and exclusion

items.text: Edward I summoned assemblies to obtain advice, hear petitions, and secure taxation. The 1295 Parliament included knights and burgesses as well as magnates and clergy. It was not modern democracy, but bargaining over money helped make representatives and recorded consent increasingly important to royal government.

Official chronology places eleven kings inside this interval, from Edward I to Henry VII. Some inherited as children, some were deposed, and some died violently. Those reign dates anchor political change, but royal sequence is not an everyday-life timeline; people planted, traded, raised families, and worshipped through several crowns.

Manorial courts recorded land transfers, local customs, debts, damaged crops, stray animals, inheritance, and obligations. Their rolls can bring ordinary disputes unusually close, yet each manor had its own practices and record survival. One grumpy pig in one roll cannot represent every medieval neighborhood.

People petitioned Chancery when they said ordinary legal remedies had failed. Surviving suits concern inheritance, marriage settlements, apprenticeships, debts, property, and trade. These stories reveal conflict and strategy, but plaintiffs shaped them to win help, so a petition is evidence with a purpose, not a secret recording.

In 1290 the crown ordered Jews out of England after decades of discriminatory law, badges, taxation, and violence. Roughly three thousand people faced dangerous journeys while houses and property passed to the crown. This was state persecution and dispossession, not a footnote to a king’s castle-building résumé.

sections.title: Cross Wales, Ireland, Gascony, and the atlas’s missing places

items.text: After Llywelyn ap Gruffudd’s death and the conquest of Gwynedd in 1282 and 1283, Edward I built castles and walled towns to control north Wales. Welsh resistance, law, language, worship, farming, and kinship did not vanish behind stone walls or beneath this atlas’s English-colored polygon.

Beaumaris Castle began in 1295 only after the crown cleared the nearby Welsh settlement of Llanfaes and forced residents to move. That makes the castle both an engineering achievement and evidence of coercion. A postcard-perfect wall can still have somebody’s demolished home underneath its origin story.

Gascon Rolls record English royal administration in Aquitaine from the thirteenth through fifteenth centuries: appointments, orders, disputes, privileges, finance, and petitions. They reveal government through paperwork and local negotiation. They do not turn every Gascon speaker, vineyard worker, merchant, or town into an English cultural copy.

Richard II’s Irish expedition used interpreters and formal submissions from more than eighty lords, yet peace soon fractured. English authority was strongest around particular towns and lordships and much weaker elsewhere. The map’s nearly island-wide component radically overstates direct, continuous control.

The target polygon also omits Calais, even though it became England’s sole remaining French bridgehead after Bordeaux fell in 1453. Meanwhile the map keeps Gascony colored English for another thirty-nine years. One boundary can therefore leave out a possession and preserve a lost one at the same time.

sections.title: Meet families, women, workers, widows, and unequal choices

items.text: Most surviving law treated married women’s legal independence differently from widows’ or single women’s, but practice varied with place, status, property, custom, and circumstance. Women farmed, brewed, traded, served, managed homes, entered religious life, defended claims, and sometimes ran businesses. “No rights” is too simple to teach.

Widowhood could bring control of property or a business, yet also debt, lawsuits, poverty, family pressure, and danger. Records preserve energetic women because they entered transactions and disputes, but many lives remain faint. Evidence of agency should not be mistaken for equal power or easy choices.

A 1341 will left forty shillings each to a son and a daughter for apprenticeships. That does not prove equal training everywhere, but it shows one family planning skilled futures for both children. Education could be money, a contract, a workshop, and years beside a craftsperson rather than a classroom.

Margaret Brotherton, born into the royal family, married at about fifteen, had four children, controlled great estates, and pursued political and marital goals. Her unusual wealth makes her a useful named life, not an average woman. Elite biographies illuminate possibilities while loudly displaying their own social bias.

Family historians face a basic gap: England had no nationwide civil register of births, marriages, and deaths in this period. Wills, courts, taxes, guilds, and land records favor people with property or official contact. A quiet family can be historically real while leaving almost no named paperwork.

sections.title: Follow children through chores, learning, toys, and written language

items.text: Children learned by watching, helping, practicing, attending school where available, and entering service or apprenticeships. Archaeology finds children’s fingerprints on pottery, while documents place some boys and girls in training. Age, wealth, location, health, and family need shaped who learned what and when.

A tiny lead-alloy jug dated broadly from the mid-thirteenth to early-fourteenth century overlaps this atlas interval only at its later end. It may have been a child’s toy for pretend household play. Fun fact: medieval children may have owned dollhouse crockery, although no child left a review saying “five stars, excellent tiny pouring.”

Girls as well as boys could enter apprenticeships, and some girls received schooling, especially in towns, elite households, or religious settings. Access was uneven. Learning also happened through food preparation, textile work, farming, worship, errands, storytelling, and care, none of which required a bell to announce class.

Written-language sample, late-fourteenth-century London English: “Whan that Aprill with his shoures soote.” Normalized reading: “When that April with his showers sweet.” Meaning: “When April with its sweet showers.” This is Chaucer’s Middle English, securely period-appropriate, but not the speech of every English, Welsh, Irish, or Gascon community.

A fifteenth-century manuscript writes the same opening with spellings such as “schowres swoote.” Medieval spelling was not standardized, and Margery Kempe composed her book through dictation to scribes. Together, these witnesses show both written variation and collaborative bookmaking. The Chaucer line remains one documented literary sample, not a universal voice.

sections.title: Enter homes, kitchens, villages, wardrobes, and working days

items.text: At West Cotton, archaeology identifies house plots, crofts, yards, paddocks, a manor, streets, and a church. Such layouts joined home, storage, animals, gardening, and work. They show one excavated settlement changing through time, not a ready-made floor plan for London, Dublin, Bordeaux, or every village.

Wharram Percy preserves houses, a mill, fishponds, church, manor, lanes, and a latrine pit. Its evidence lets families explore an actual village landscape, yet the settlement changed over centuries. Archaeology is strongest when “people lived like this” becomes “people at this named place left these traces.”

Goodrich Castle accounts show a large household of relatives, guests, officials, and servants consuming food and organizing repairs. One account lists eighty-one pigs, which is less a cute petting zoo than a serious meat supply. Elite abundance should not be projected onto neighboring cottages.

Castle kitchens handled bread, meat, fish, drink, fuel, storage, serving, and mountains of washing-up. Bread quality marked rank, while cooks and servants worked long hours. A feast looked glamorous from the high table because somebody else had already met the onions, smoke, grease, and dishwater.

Long-toed poulaines became fashionable in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Surviving shoes and criticism show both craft and social anxiety around dress. Pointy toes could signal style, but they did not make walking through mud magically dignified. Clothing evidence is strongest in particular finds and texts.

sections.title: Move wool, wine, people, money, and disputes

items.text: Wool was England’s leading medieval export, while cloth, wine, and many other goods passed through ports. Customs accounts name merchants, cargoes, ships, origins, destinations, and payments. They document taxable trade especially well; smuggling, tiny exchanges, unpaid household labor, and goods that escaped the clerk remain harder to count.

Records from 1330 to 1550 contain tens of thousands of immigrant names from many places and occupations. Some newcomers formed households, married, served, crafted, traded, or studied. “Foreign” was a legal and fiscal category, not a complete personality, and one tax list cannot capture every migrant.

Manorial accounts connect fields, mills, rents, harvest labor, livestock, officials, and markets. Court rolls show neighbors enforcing custom and disputing land or debts. They can make a village look paperwork-heavy, but most conversations, favors, jokes, recipes, and acts of care never reached the roll.

Chancery petitions expose broken deals among merchants, apprentices, spouses, heirs, lenders, and partners. Because petitioners emphasized unfairness, historians compare claims with replies and other records. Medieval people understood strategic storytelling perfectly well; adding “most wronged person in England” to a complaint was not a neutral survey response.

Wills identify selected possessions, gifts, debts, relatives, charities, executors, and burial wishes. They illuminate material and social ties but survive unevenly, especially favoring wealthier people and southern jurisdictions. An object omitted from a will was not necessarily absent from a home, unloved, or unimportant.

sections.title: Treat sickness, live with disability, and investigate plague

items.text: Medieval hospitals might offer shelter, food, nursing, prayer, and long-term support rather than modern diagnosis and emergency surgery. Some separated men and women; some served particular groups. Care mixed physical, social, and spiritual aims, and disability did not produce one universal institution or life path.

The After the Plague project studies skeletons from the cemetery of Cambridge’s Hospital of St John to investigate diet, disease, injury, migration, and poverty. These people provide direct biological evidence, but each body belongs to one person and one institution, not a medical average for the entire atlas.

John of Arderne wrote an illustrated surgical work in the fourteenth century and described treating anal fistula. The manuscript shows observation, instruments, recipes, and professional self-presentation. It also answers a timeless question: yes, medieval surgeons wrote seriously about bottoms, because painful problems do not become less real when history books feel embarrassed.

During the Black Death, physicians explained illness through humors, environment, astrology, or corrupted air and might use bloodletting or herbal remedies. Many people could not afford a physician. Their theories differed from germ theory, but care, fear, observation, prayer, and practical nursing were not the same as doing nothing.

Chemical testing of vessels from the infirmary at Spitalfields found residues including lead and mercury. The report is technical and preliminary, so residues do not automatically reveal one prescription, dose, or patient. Laboratory evidence can narrow possibilities while still requiring context, chronology, and healthy caution about poisonous ingredients.

sections.title: Answer the water, waste, bathing, and toilet questions honestly

items.text: Castles used garderobes whose seats opened into shafts, pits, moats, or outside walls. Location, cleaning, water, and status varied. A grand castle could have impressive masonry and an extremely direct relationship with gravity. “Medieval toilet” therefore names several arrangements, not one universal porcelain-free design.

Waste pits and garderobes needed emptying, and specialized workers sometimes removed accumulated filth. The job could be dangerous, smelly, and essential. Calling the workers “gong farmers” may delight children, but the useful lesson is urban infrastructure: somebody always has to make the sanitation system continue working.

A 1328 London dispute described waste leaking from one household’s cesspit into a neighbor’s cellar. That single case proves neither universal filth nor effective sewerage. It does show household sanitation, property rights, smell, damage, and neighborly fury colliding in a record vivid enough to survive.

London authorities also confronted blocked gutters and waste in streets. Rules and complaints show that people cared about drainage and nuisance even when enforcement failed. The city was not cheerfully swimming in muck; it was repeatedly arguing about who must move the muck, where, and at whose expense.

London Museum records a medieval three-seat wooden toilet, while castles could also have multi-seat privies. Several users might sit side by side, so toilet privacy depended on place, building, and rank. The funniest safe fact is architectural: some medieval bathrooms treated “personal space” as an optional upgrade.

sections.title: Make books and glass, practice faith, count achievements, and continue

items.text: Paper manuscripts circulated in England before printing, although paper was imported and parchment remained important. Scribes, parchmenters, papermakers abroad, merchants, binders, illuminators, readers, and libraries formed a knowledge supply chain. A book was an intellectual object and also an engineered stack of costly materials and labor.

William Caxton brought printing to Westminster in 1476 and worked as printer, publisher, translator, and bookseller. Westminster Abbey says he published a hundred books between 1473 and his death. His press was a major achievement built from movable type, ink, paper, finance, language choices, skilled labor, and customers.

York Minster’s Great East Window was commissioned from John Thornton in 1405 and made in about three years. Its scale celebrates design, glass painting, stonework, scaffolding, organization, and teams of workers. Naming the master matters, but so do the many hands that made a wall of pictures stand and shine.

Parish churches organized worship, calendars, gatherings, charity, memory, and local status, while pilgrimage connected people and places. Criticism also grew, including Lollard challenges to church authority. Medieval religion was neither one unchanging belief nor mere superstition; it structured communities and also generated disagreement, exclusion, and reform.

Bosworth in 1485 ended Richard III’s reign and began Henry VII’s, but dynastic victory did not end England, Wales, Ireland, or Gascony as lived places. Achievements in government, craft, care, trade, writing, farming, and art belonged to many people, including those absent from royal stories.

ending.text: The atlas removes “english-territory” at 1492. Sampled English and Welsh points, Dublin, and Cork switch to “england-1492,” while Bordeaux and Bayonne switch to France; the same assignments remain in 1500. Henry VII’s kingdom continued, as did Welsh, Irish, French, and Gascon communities and their distinct histories. Bosworth had changed the ruling dynasty in 1485, not erased the population. This ending records an atlas relabeling and a long-delayed territorial correction, not a civilization’s fall.
